name: Aho-Corasick Automaton & Multi-Pattern Matching
tagline: Compile K signatures into a single Trie with BFS Failure & Output Links to match all patterns in one O(N + M + Z) linear pass.
purpose: Eliminate O(K * N) sequential regex or KMP scans in WAF, DLP, and content-moderation pipelines by pre-compiling dictionaries into a deterministic multi-pattern automaton.

spark.summary: The Aho-Corasick Automaton fuses a prefix Trie with KMP-style BFS failure links and dictionary output links, scanning N-byte payloads against K patterns in O(N + M + Z) amortized time.
spark.keyTakeaway: To keep storage layouts predictable as data grows, by pre-computing fallback suffix transitions once during compilation, per-request matching time becomes completely independent of dictionary size K.
spark.byteSummary:
Core Mechanics & Why Sequential Scans Fail: When a Web Application Firewall (WAF) or Data Loss Prevention (DLP) engine checks a 10 KB payload against K = 10,000 banned signatures using sequential KMP or regex loops, it performs O(K * N) = 100 million character comparisons per request—saturating 64-core nodes below 500 req/s. Aho-Corasick solves this by compiling all K patterns (total length M) into a single prefix Trie upfront.

BFS Failure Links & Dictionary Output Links: During a breadth-first traversal (BFS) over the Trie, each node u stores a failure link fail(u) pointing to the longest proper suffix of u's prefix that also exists in the Trie. Whenever a pattern ends inside another pattern (such as 'he' inside 'she'), output links (or pre-merged output lists) ensure every overlapping match is reported without backtracking the input pointer.

Amortized O(N + M + Z) Guarantee & Failure Modes: Because the current Trie depth increases by at most 1 per input character and each failure-link hop strictly decreases depth by at least 1, the potential argument proves at most 2N total state transitions for any N-byte input, plus Z reported matches. In production, engineers must guard against unbounded alphabet fan-out (using compact arrays or double-array tries for ASCII/UTF-8) and swap immutable compiled automata atomically to avoid mid-request mutation races.

learningJourney.title: The Multi-Pattern Bottleneck: Why O(K * N) Collapses
learningJourney.purpose: Quantify why running single-pattern algorithms (KMP, Boyer-Moore, or individual regexes) K times saturates CPU on high-throughput inspection pipelines.

explanation.foundation: Single-pattern algorithms like Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) scan an N-character payload in O(N) time. However, security and moderation systems rarely search for one keyword—they evaluate K = 10,000+ signatures concurrently. Looping KMP or compiled regular expressions over each pattern forces K full memory passes over the payload, inflating CPU cache misses and driving work to O(K * N) = 10^8 operations per 10 KB request.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Aho-Corasick Automaton & Multi-Pattern Matching, watch how the multi-pattern bottleneck: why o(k * n) collapses interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. Production WAF/DLP engines flatten Aho-Corasick into a complete DFA transition table or Double-Array Trie and hot-swap immutable instances atomically.

learningJourney.purpose: Build the goto-function Trie so shared pattern prefixes are represented once in memory.

explanation.foundation: The first phase of Aho-Corasick inserts all K patterns (with total character length M) into a standard Trie. Shared prefixes such as 'he' and 'hers' share the exact same root->h->e path, bounding total Trie nodes to at most M + 1.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Aho-Corasick Automaton & Multi-Pattern Matching without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: To keep storage layouts predictable as data grows, by pre-computing fallback suffix transitions once during compilation, per-request matching time becomes completely independent of dictionary size K.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: BFS Failure Links: Generalizing KMP's Prefix Function
learningJourney.purpose: Compute fail(v) via breadth-first search so mismatches jump to the longest valid suffix state without rewinding the text pointer.

explanation.foundation: If we match 'sh' and the next character is 'i' (no 'i' child from 'sh'), we must not rewind the input tape; 'h' is already matched as a suffix of 'sh'! A BFS starting from depth-1 children (whose fail link is always root) computes fail(v) for each child v = u.next[ch] by walking f = u.fail until f has a transition on ch or f reaches None (defaulting to root). Because BFS processes nodes in strictly increasing depth order, every shallower fail target is already finalized.

learningJourney.title: Dictionary Output Links: Catching Embedded Sub-Matches
learningJourney.purpose: Ensure patterns that end strictly inside another pattern (like 'he' inside 'she' or 'ushers') are never missed.

explanation.foundation: Consider the text 'ushers' with patterns {'he', 'she', 'hers'}. When the automaton reaches state 'she', it must report both 'she' AND its proper suffix 'he'. There are two equivalent ways to achieve this: (1) pre-merge v.outputs.extend(v.fail.outputs) during BFS (simple and O(1) lookup if output lists are small), or (2) store a compressed dictionary-suffix pointer dict_link(v) pointing to the nearest ancestor along the fail chain that has non-empty outputs, keeping build space strictly O(M) even when many patterns nest.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Aho-Corasick Automaton & Multi-Pattern Matching, watch how dictionary output links: catching embedded sub-matches interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. Production WAF/DLP engines flatten Aho-Corasick into a complete DFA transition table or Double-Array Trie and hot-swap immutable instances atomically.

learningJourney.title: Amortized O(N + M + Z) Proof via Potential Method
learningJourney.purpose: Prove formally why the while-loop following failure links cannot degrade runtime to O(N * M).

explanation.foundation: At first glance, the inner `while cur is not root and ch not in cur.next: cur = cur.fail` loop looks like it could run many times on a single character.
explanation.core: Define the potential function Phi(cur) = depth(cur) in the Trie. Initially Phi = 0 and Phi >= 0 always. In each outer loop iteration (one per input character, N total), `cur = cur.next.get(ch, root)` increases depth by at most +1.
explanation.deepDive: Every execution of `cur = cur.fail` strictly decreases depth by at least -1 (since fail(cur) is a proper suffix of cur). Therefore, across all N characters, total failure-link traversals cannot exceed N, bounding total transitions at <= 2N and total runtime at O(N + M + Z).

sectionDiagram.title: Potential Function Phi = depth(cur) <= 2N Transitions

cards.label: Independent of K
cards.detail: Whether K = 10 or K = 100,000 patterns, character transitions stay <= 2N.

cards.label: Worst-Case Per-Char
cards.detail: A single character can take O(L_max) fail steps, but only after L_max prior +1 advances.

sectionDiagram.summary: Caption: The potential function Phi = depth(cur) proves total state transitions are strictly bounded by 2N.

learningJourney.title: DFA Completion & Double-Array Tries for Cache-Line Speed
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate the inner while-loop entirely and compress pointer-chasing hash maps into flat integer arrays for 50k+ req/s WAF nodes.

explanation.foundation: In latency-critical C++, Rust, or Java WAFs, following `dict` hash maps and inner `while` loops causes CPU branch mispredictions and pointer-chasing cache misses.
explanation.core: During BFS, we can pre-compute the complete deterministic transition table `go[u][c]` for every byte `c` in `0..255`: if `c` is a Trie child, `go[u][c] = child`; otherwise `go[u][c] = go[fail[u]][c]`.
explanation.deepDive: This turns scanning into a branch-free `state = go[state][byte]` lookup in O(1) worst-case per byte—or, to save memory on large alphabets, a Double-Array Trie (DAT) storing `base[]` and `check[]` arrays.

sectionDiagram.title: Complete DFA Transition Table vs Pointer-Chasing Trie

cards.label: Memory vs Speed
cards.detail: Full 256-byte table uses 1 KB/state (e.g., 100 MB for 100k states) for zero-branch O(1) transitions.

cards.label: Double-Array Trie
cards.detail: Packs sparse byte transitions into contiguous int32 base/check arrays.

learningJourney.title: Zero-Downtime Hot-Reloading & Production Failure Modes
learningJourney.purpose: Safely update threat signatures in live traffic without mutating the active automaton or triggering OOM.

explanation.foundation: Production WAFs update rulesets every few minutes. Mutating a live Trie in place causes torn reads and segfaults/NPEs across worker threads. Instead, compile new signatures in a background builder thread with bounded memory limits, verify automaton size, and atomically swap an immutable reference (`AtomicReference` / `ArcSwap`).

knowledgeChecks.question: In an Aho-Corasick Automaton, why must failure links be computed in Breadth-First Search (BFS) order rather than Depth-First Search (DFS) order?

options.text: DFS cannot traverse Trie edges that contain ASCII characters.
options.feedback: Incorrect: DFS can traverse any edge, but it visits deep nodes before their shallower suffix targets are computed.

options.text: Because fail(v) always points to a strictly shallower node, BFS guarantees every candidate suffix state already has its failure link finalized.
options.feedback: Correct: Since depth(fail(u)) < depth(u), level-order BFS ensures all shallower failure links are ready when computing v.fail.

options.text: BFS reduces the number of Trie nodes from O(M) to O(log M).
options.feedback: Incorrect: The number of Trie states is determined by the shared prefixes (up to M+1), not by the traversal order.

options.text: DFS would skip reporting overlapping patterns at the root.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Overlapping patterns are handled by output links, while BFS is required specifically for failure-link dependency order.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Because fail(u) always has strictly smaller depth than u, BFS guarantees all shallower failure links are finalized before deeper nodes depend on them.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which potential-function argument proves that the Aho-Corasick search phase performs at most 2N state transitions on an N-character text?

options.text: Each failure-link hop doubles the alphabet size.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Failure-link hops do not change the alphabet size.

options.text: The Trie depth decreases by 1 on every forward edge.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Forward Trie edges increase depth by +1.

options.text: Depth Phi(cur) increases by at most +1 per input character and strictly decreases by at least 1 on each failure-link hop, with Phi >= 0.
options.feedback: Correct: With at most N total +1 increments and Phi >= 0, there can be at most N failure-link decrements, bounding total transitions at <= 2N.

options.text: Every pattern in the dictionary has length <= 2.
options.feedback: Incorrect: The 2N bound holds for arbitrary pattern lengths M.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Depth increases by at most 1 per character (N times total) and drops by at least 1 per failure hop, so failure hops cannot exceed N.

knowledgeChecks.question: With patterns {'he', 'she', 'hers'} and input 'ushers', what ensures 'he' is still reported when the automaton reaches state 'she'?

options.text: Dictionary output links (or pre-merged output lists) inherit matches from fail('she') -> 'he'.
options.feedback: Correct: 'he' is a proper suffix of 'she', so output propagation along failure links emits both 'she' and 'he' at index 3.

options.text: The scanner rewinds the input pointer back 2 characters after matching 'she'.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Aho-Corasick never rewinds the input pointer.

options.text: The root node stores all patterns in a sorted array.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Outputs are attached to accepting and suffix-linked states, not scanned from root.

options.text: KMP prefix tables are re-run after each match.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Output links resolve embedded matches in O(1) per match without re-running KMP.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Output links (or pre-merged outputs along failure links) propagate accepting states from proper suffixes like 'he' into 'she'.

beginner.summary: Aho-Corasick lets you search a document for thousands of keywords in a single left-to-right pass instead of checking one keyword at a time.
beginner.keyTakeaway: To keep storage layouts predictable as data grows, by pre-computing fallback suffix transitions once during compilation, per-request matching time becomes completely independent of dictionary size K.
beginner.byteSummary: Instead of scanning a 10 KB message 10,000 separate times for 10,000 banned words, Aho-Corasick merges all words into one prefix tree. When a letter doesn't match, a pre-computed failure arrow jumps to the longest matching suffix already seen, keeping the scan strictly one pass.

intermediate.summary: Aho-Corasick compiles K patterns of total length M into a Trie, computes BFS failure and output links in O(M) time, and scans N-byte text in O(N + Z) amortized time.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: To keep storage layouts predictable as data grows, by pre-computing fallback suffix transitions once during compilation, per-request matching time becomes completely independent of dictionary size K.
intermediate.byteSummary: By combining a prefix Trie with BFS-computed failure links and output links, Aho-Corasick generalizes KMP from 1 pattern to K patterns. Build time is O(M * |Sigma|) (or O(M) with hash/array maps) and search time is O(N + Z), where Z is the number of matches.

advanced.summary: Production WAF/DLP engines flatten Aho-Corasick into a complete DFA transition table or Double-Array Trie and hot-swap immutable instances atomically.
advanced.keyTakeaway: To keep storage layouts predictable as data grows, by pre-computing fallback suffix transitions once during compilation, per-request matching time becomes completely independent of dictionary size K.
advanced.byteSummary: At 50,000+ req/s, pointer-chasing Trie nodes and variable failure-link chains cause cache misses and tail-latency jitter. Flattening transitions into a byte-indexed DFA (or compact Double-Array Trie) and compiling rule updates in a background thread for atomic pointer swap achieves predictable sub-millisecond inspection.
